description: 🚀 Team Space Design Challenge | We are a team of 6 locked in for the challenge! Bringing together Information Management, Financial Analysis, Data Modeling, Python/SQL, and Systems Design. We bridge high-level strategy and technical execution to build feasible, data-driven space solutions. Excited to innovate, connect with mentors, and take on the future of space architecture! 🌌
summary: We developed a free, browser-based 2D strategy game set in the Cold War space race (1955–1969). Each player runs a space agency (USA or USSR side) racing to complete a ladder of historical missions. A dice-driven circular board provides resources, buildings, shops, espionage and chance events — but the heart of the game is the engineering workshop: players design their spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, orbit, instruments and parts, each with explicit trade-offs in cost, mass, power, data and risk, then decide the central dilemma — launch now, cheap and risky, or wait and let rivals pull ahead. Launches are simulated stage by stage, and every failure comes with a clear explanation of why it happened, plus a "In real history" card connecting it to actual events. This addresses the challenge directly: players define mission goals, design under constraints, simulate, and learn from feedback. It matters because it makes real mission-design reasoning — budgets, trade-offs, risk — accessible and fun for beginners and youth, solo or with up to four players, with no installation required.
details:
What it does / how it works: A browser-based 2D board game where 1–4 players each run a space agency (US/USSR) during the 1955–1969 space race. Gameplay alternates between a shared circular board (dice movement, buildings, shops, espionage, chance events, rival bots) and an engineering workshop where players design spacecraft — picking launch vehicles, orbits, instruments, and parts, each with explicit cost/mass/power/data/risk trade-offs. Each turn, players choose to research, build, upgrade, or attempt launch. Launches run through a staged simulation (src/sim/simulate.js, flight.js) that computes success/failure with transparent causes, tied to a historical "In real history" card. Years advance in 3-round cycles (1955→1969), building a ladder of missions players race to complete first.

Benefits: No installs, no cost, runs entirely in-browser; supports solo (sandbox) or hot-seat/networked multiplayer up to 4; teaches real mission-design reasoning (budget, mass, power, data, risk) through consequence rather than lecture; failure is explained, not just penalized, turning mistakes into learning moments.

Intended impact: Make space mission engineering trade-offs approachable and engaging for beginners/youth, per the challenge's goal of broadening access to mission design concepts, while also teaching real space race history.

Tools/languages: Plain JavaScript (ES modules), no build step/framework, node --test for testing; custom peer-to-peer networking (src/net/peer.js, lobby.js, sync.js, roomCode.js) for multiplayer; HTML/CSS for UI/rendering (src/ui/*, src/board/board.js).

Creativity: Combines a Monopoly-style board (resource/social layer) with a serious engineering/simulation layer underneath; frames the core tension as "launch now (cheap, risky) vs. wait (safer, rivals advance)"; adds narrative texture via espionage, rumors, dilemma cards, and historical callouts tying game outcomes to real Cold War space history.

Factors considered: Every mechanic was checked against whether it affects the core launch-now-vs-wait decision (cut if it's just flavor); balance was tuned to avoid snowballing (rising upgrade costs, discounts for players who fall behind); the team was explicit about not fabricating real rocket/instrument/mission data — approximated balance values are flagged as such in code/docs.
